images.about-crayon.png: Use case: illustration-story. Asset type: illustration for the Marine tier of MANET mesh-radio documentation, the very first page, explaining what a mesh radio does to a second grader. Make a landscape 1536 by 1024 wax-crayon drawing on warm white paper, convincingly drawn by a SECOND GRADER: wobbly outlines, wonky proportions, inconsistent scale, loose scribbled fills with paper showing, overshoots, thick wax texture. Not polished vector art or professional cartoon art. Generous blank space. Scene: an outdoor landscape with a few scribbly green trees and one brown hill. Three simple stick-figure friends stand far apart across the page (left, middle on the hill, right), each holding a small phone, each next to the SAME plain olive green rectangular radio box with two short black antennas (a schematic symbol, not a real product). Orange dashed curved lines hop from the left radio to the middle radio and from the middle radio to the right radio, showing a message being passed along. In the far background, a small gray cell tower with a big red crayon X scribbled over it. A crooked yellow sun in a corner. No text, labels, speech bubbles, logos or watermarks except optionally one backwards letter scribble. No weapons, camouflage, uniforms, helmets or military imagery. Friendly, simple and legible. Critical layout: put each friend to the LEFT of their own radio, with the middle friend lower on the left slope of the hill and the middle radio alone on the hilltop. Leave clear blank space immediately above all three radios. Draw exactly two complete orange dashed arches: one directly connecting the antennas of the left and middle radios, and another directly connecting the antennas of the middle and right radios. Both arches must visibly meet the middle radio's antennas, with no person, phone, tree or gap hiding either endpoint. The phones do not connect to the orange arches. Keep trees outside the radio-to-radio paths and keep the lower paper mostly blank.

images.first-boot-crayon.png: Use case: illustration-story. Asset type: an instructional illustration for the Marine tier of MANET mesh-radio documentation. Make one landscape page containing four clearly separated crayon drawings in a simple 2 by 2 arrangement, read left to right then down. The drawings must look convincingly made by a young child with real wax crayons on warm white paper: wobbly outlines, uneven proportions, scribbled fills that leave paper showing, little overshoots, visible chunky wax texture. Charming, extremely simple and legible, not polished vector art or professional cartoon art. Use the SAME plain olive green rectangular mesh-radio box with two short black antennas in every panel; this is a schematic symbol, not a realistic product. Panel 1: a blue Ethernet cable connects a small home internet router to the green radio. Panel 2: a black cable from a wall power adapter connects to the radio. Panel 3: the radio beside a large simple clock and a curved looping arrow, conveying waiting through restarts while cables stay connected. Panel 4: a close-up of the radio with one GREEN indicator glowing, short repeated green dash marks suggesting a heartbeat blink; the other indicator is dark. Keep plenty of white space between panels so they are visually distinct. Only a small crayon numeral 1, 2, 3, 4 at the top left of each panel; no other text, labels, speech bubbles, logos, checkmarks, watermarks, or faces. No weapons, camouflage, people, helmets, or military imagery. This should look like a child's drawing explaining useful radio setup, not a joke about the reader. Use clear blue for Ethernet, black for power, green for the same radio and the final LED. Output a 1536 by 1024 landscape image if possible.

images.features-crayon.png:
Create one landscape 1536 × 1024 PNG illustration for the Marine tier of the MANET field guide’s features list. A second grader should be able to tell that the radios help people talk, find each other on a map, share internet, and pass messages across a group.

Draw on warm white paper with wax crayons. Make it look like a real second grader drew it: wobbly outlines, wonky proportions, uneven shapes, scribbled fills with bits of paper showing, overshoots, and thick wax texture. Keep it friendly, simple, and easy to understand. Leave generous blank space. Avoid polished vector art and professional cartoon art.

Show three friends in different parts of a simple outdoor scene. Place one olive-green radio beside each friend. Keep all three radios the same: a plain rectangular box with two short black antennas, drawn as a simple symbol rather than a realistic product.

Use orange dashed curves to connect the radios, showing that messages can pass between them. Beside one friend, draw a phone with a simple map and three little dots for the friends’ locations. Beside another, draw a headset and a small push-to-talk button. Beside the third, draw a simple router with a blue internet cloud above it and an orange dashed link from the router to that friend’s radio. Make each idea clear, with plenty of space between the objects.

Use blue only for the cable between the router and its radio. Use orange dashed curves only for wireless links between radios. Do not draw a cell tower or cross it out. Do not reuse the hilltop relay scene with three friends holding phones. Include no text, labels, speech bubbles, logos, or watermarks. Include no weapons, camouflage, uniforms, or military imagery.
